title: H3 – Recruitment and selection: designing the process
source: Zusammenfassung von Session 2 „Recruitment and selection“ (Inditex-Fall, CIPD 2026)

blocks.text: Recruitment attracts the right pool of candidates; selection applies techniques to identify the right candidates out of that pool. Good recruitment makes selection possible.
Selection methods must be valid (measure what predicts performance in the job), reliable (consistent) and practicable (cost, time, acceptance).
A strong recommendation starts from the job description, considers person–organisation fit and the local context, explains why the methods are valid, reliable and practicable, and is cost-effective.
Recruitment balances the organisation's and the candidate's needs – informing vs attracting – and should consider internal recruitment.
More applications do not mean better candidates (CIPD 2026).
Staffing process
Selection criteria
Recruitment strategy choices
Checklist for a selection strategy (Inditex feedback)
children: Which aspect of performance in the job description does each method measure?
How do the methods work together to increase validity and reliability?
Repetitions: do methods measure the same criteria – necessary and cost-effective?
Coverage: are all relevant requirements evaluated?

blocks.text: Evidence (CIPD 2026)
children: 58 % more applications but only 33 % more suitable candidates
Top methods: own website 40 %, job boards 35 %, internal advertising 32 %
Median cost per hire: £3,500 senior, £2,000 other employees

blocks.text: 1. Analyse the job description: key tasks, competencies, context (country, level).
2. Recruitment: target pool, channels, internal option, message (inform AND attract), cost.
3. Selection: build a method-by-criterion grid – each requirement covered, each method justified on validity, reliability and practicability.
4. Close with cost-effectiveness and fit with the employer brand.
Activities that attract a pool of suitable candidates for a vacancy.
Applying techniques to choose the most suitable candidate(s) from the pool.
The degree to which a selection method measures what it is meant to measure – i.e. predicts job performance.
The consistency of a method's results across raters, occasions and candidates.
Whether a method is feasible: cost, time, administrative effort, candidate acceptance, legality.
Compatibility between a person's values and goals and those of the organisation.
Why might the same firm (Inditex) need different recruitment strategies for positions in different countries?
